guide.title: Period 7 (1890–1945): review guide
guide.intro: In Period 7 the United States became a world power, reformers tried to tame industrial capitalism, the 1920s brought new technology and culture wars, and the Great Depression and two world wars vastly expanded the federal government's role. Comparison is the period's key reasoning skill.

sections.title: Imperialism, world wars, and diplomacy
body: After the Spanish–American War (1898) the United States acquired Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines, where it fought a long war against Filipino independence forces; it also annexed Hawaii. Anti-imperialists argued that colonies betrayed American principles. The United States entered World War I in 1917; afterward the Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles and the League of Nations, and the nation largely avoided foreign commitments in the 1920s and 1930s.

After Pearl Harbor (December 1941), the United States fought in Europe and the Pacific; the war ended in 1945 after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Wartime and postwar diplomacy led to the United Nations and set the stage for tension with the Soviet Union.
points: Comparison: debates over involvement after WWI vs. global leadership after WWII.
Imperialism was justified by economic, strategic, and racial arguments.

sections.title: Progressives, the WWI home front, and the 1920s
body: Progressives used journalism (muckrakers), science, and government to address problems of industrial society: unsafe factories (the Triangle Shirtwaist fire of 1911 led to New York safety laws), corrupt politics, monopolies, and impure food. Constitutional amendments brought the income tax, direct election of senators, Prohibition, and women's suffrage (1920). During World War I, the government restricted dissent (Espionage and Sedition Acts), and the Great Migration of African Americans to Northern cities began.

In the 1920s, radio, film, and automobiles created a national mass culture. Conflicts arose over immigration (quota laws of 1921 and 1924), Prohibition, evolution (the Scopes trial, 1925), and race; the Harlem Renaissance celebrated African American culture.
points: Progressives were mostly middle-class reformers who trusted expertise and government.

sections.title: The Great Depression, the New Deal, and mobilization
body: The stock market crash of 1929 and bank failures deepened a depression that left about a quarter of workers unemployed by 1933. Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal used relief, recovery, and reform: a bank holiday and deposit insurance (FDIC), work programs, Social Security (1935), and protection for unions (the Wagner Act). Critics on the left said it did too little, and on the right that it expanded government too far.

World War II mobilization ended the Depression: factories converted to war production, women and African Americans took new jobs, and Mexican workers came through the Bracero Program. Wartime also brought injustice, most notably the forced removal and incarceration of Japanese Americans under Executive Order 9066 (1942).
points: Compare the Progressive Era and the New Deal: both expanded government, but the New Deal was far larger.
Mobilization, not the New Deal alone, ended mass unemployment.

example.prompt: Compare the Progressive movement and the New Deal in one sentence.
example.solution: Both used government to address problems of industrial capitalism, but the Progressives worked mostly through state and local reforms and regulation, while the New Deal created large federal programs of relief, recovery, and social insurance in response to an economic emergency.

misconceptions: “The United States was isolationist throughout the interwar years.”
It avoided alliances but stayed active in trade, investment, and diplomacy.
“The New Deal ended the Great Depression.”
It eased hardship, but wartime mobilization ended mass unemployment.
Most were middle-class reformers who wanted to fix, not replace, capitalism.

passages.title: Source A: An eyewitness account of the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire, 1911
text: “I saw every feature of the tragedy visible from outside the building. I learned a new sound—a more horrible sound than description can picture. It was the thud of a speeding, living body on a stone sidewalk. . . . I looked upon the heap of dead bodies and I remembered these girls were the shirtwaist makers. I remembered their great strike of last year in which these same girls had demanded more sanitary conditions and more safety precautions in the shops. These dead bodies were the answer.”
passages.attribution: William Shepherd, a United Press reporter who witnessed the fire in New York City on March 25, 1911, telephoning his account to his news service. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 21.2.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published before 1931, or a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/21-2-progressivism-at-the-grassroots-level); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source B: Franklin D. Roosevelt, radio address on banking, 1933
text: “I recognize that the many proclamations from State capitols and from Washington, the legislation, the Treasury regulations, etc., couched for the most part in banking and legal terms, should be explained for the benefit of the average citizen. . . . After all, there is an element in the readjustment of our financial system more important than currency, more important than gold, and that is the confidence of the people. Confidence and courage are the essentials of success in carrying out our plan. You people must have faith; you must not be stampeded by rumors or guesses. Let us unite in banishing fear. We have provided the machinery to restore our financial system; it is up to you to support and make it work.”
passages.attribution: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, his first radio “fireside chat,” March 12, 1933. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 26.2.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published before 1931, or a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/26-2-the-first-new-deal); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source C: An interpretation of the debate over empire, 1898–1902
text: “The war with Spain in 1898 lasted only months, but the peace raised questions Americans argued about for years. Expansionists pointed to markets in Asia, coaling stations for a modern navy, and what they called a duty to “civilize” other peoples. Anti-imperialists, a group that included Mark Twain, Andrew Carnegie, and Jane Addams, answered that ruling the Philippines without the consent of Filipinos betrayed the principles of the Declaration of Independence. The bloody war against Filipino independence fighters that followed seemed to many of them to prove their point.”

passages.title: Source D: An interpretation of the home front in World War II
text: “World War II transformed American society more than any event since the Civil War. Factories that had stood idle in the Depression ran around the clock, unemployment nearly disappeared, and millions of women took industrial jobs once reserved for men. African Americans moved to war-industry cities and launched the “Double V” campaign for victory over fascism abroad and racism at home. Yet the same government that called the war a fight for freedom forced more than 100,000 Japanese Americans, most of them citizens, from their homes into incarceration camps.”
